problem: Hierarchical navigation methods either need precise high-level information (accurate maps) given in advance, or learn a topological map from experience in the training environment, so they do not generalize to novel environments without further learning.
motivation: Robots must generalize quickly to new places without building accurate occupancy maps first. Humans navigate novel places from a rough 2-D map by planning landmarks and reaching them one by one. The authors want the same: a cheap, rough, possibly imprecise map for high-level guidance plus a reusable local controller trained only on local behaviors.
key_idea: Initialize an optimistic dynamic topological graph from a rough 2-D map, plan landmarks on it, use a map-patch-conditioned CVAE to hallucinate first-person landmark observations as subgoals for a local goal-conditioned double DQN, and delete graph edges when the controller fails.
insight: The ablation on 15x15 seen mazes shows both parts matter: open-loop A* path following on the 2-D map (our-2d-map) drops performance significantly, and with no map (our-no-map) navigation at distance >=5 almost always fails. Local behaviors (crossing an intersection, turning at a corner) transfer across mazes, so the global structure can come from a rough map. Map errors up to about 10% are tolerated because replanning routes around failures.
method: Dynamic topological map: directed graph whose nodes are feasible 3x3 local map patches of the rough 2-D map, optimistically initialized with bidirectional edges between neighbouring free cells. An edge is deleted when the controller fails to traverse it, then Dijkstra replans (closed loop).

Landmark observation generator: CVAE conditioned on a 3x3 binary map patch and an 8-way one-hot direction, with a 64-D latent and 32x32 RGB output. Trained on ~22k random-policy images from mazes <=13x13. Panoramic subgoals are built from 8 directional generations.

Local controller: goal-conditioned double DQN on panoramic observation plus goal observation, trained on local behaviors in one maze for 1M steps. Goals are relabeled with generated observations in 50% of cases.

Landmark-reached detection: the 'pred' variant adds a binary-classification head (cross-entropy loss) to predict whether the current observation matches the subgoal. The 'oracle' variant gets this signal from the environment.

Planning loop: the graph outputs only the first landmark on the shortest path. If the landmark is not reached, the agent returns to the previous landmark, the edge is removed and a new path is planned, all within a 100-step budget.

setting.backbone: CVAE (conv encoder/decoder, from scratch) + goal-conditioned double DQN (ConvNet, from scratch)
setting.training_data: CVAE: ~22k random-policy 32x32 RGB images labeled with map patch and direction from DeepMind Lab mazes <=13x13. DQN: 1M steps in a single maze (generalization tests); optionally 5 mazes.
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (8 directions, 32x32) plus a rough 2-D binary occupancy map
setting.action_space: 4 discrete tile moves (up/down/left/right); harder variant with acceleration actions
setting.privileged: none at test time beyond the rough 2-D map (the oracle variant uses environment landmark-reached signal; start/goal given as map positions)

numbers_note: Main results are only in figures (success rate vs start-goal distance per maze size); no per-benchmark table with canonical metrics. Only appendix Table 1 (generalization to larger mazes) is numeric, and it is not a standard benchmark entry.
results: On DeepMind Lab discrete mazes, the method beats HER and Map Planner in seen mazes (except 13x13, where Map Planner using true state is best) and in unseen mazes, where all methods are trained on one maze and tested zero-shot on the other 19. In unseen mazes it reaches about 90% success for distance <=3 (HER 78%), while Map Planner fails beyond distance 10. Trained on one 15x15 maze, it reaches 77.2% success at distance <=10 on larger mazes and 35.1% at 20-35.
limitations: Evaluated only in synthetic DeepMind Lab mazes with 32x32 images and simplified discrete actions; the continuous-control variant degrades.
Fails when the rough map has >=30% errors and can't discover behaviors the map deems impossible; one-directional edges bottleneck long-distance navigation.
Controller trained on one maze lacks some local behaviors, so long-distance success in larger mazes declines.
